items: Acute Dystonia: Involuntary muscular contractions, torticollis, oculogyric crisis, trismus, laryngeal spasm (DSM p.812)
Acute Akathisia: Subjective inner restlessness in legs plus observed movements like pacing, leg swinging, rocking (DSM p.813)
Parkinsonism: Bradykinesia, lead-pipe or cogwheel rigidity, 3-6 Hz resting tremor, masked facies, shuffling gait (DSM p.808)
High D2 receptor occupancy (>80%) in dorsal striatum triggers motor EPS (StahlNeuro p.165)
Children, adolescents, and young males under 40 are at highest risk for acute dystonia (DSM p.812, Dulcan p.819, StahlKids p.39)
key_numbers: 50% of acute dystonia cases occur within 24-48 hours (DSM p.812)
90% of acute dystonia cases occur within 5 days (DSM p.812)
>80% D2 occupancy threshold in dorsal striatum for EPS (StahlNeuro p.165)
20%-75% prevalence of akathisia in patients on antipsychotics (DSM p.814)
50% of outpatients on chronic FGAs develop parkinsonism (DSM p.808)

clusters.name: Medication-Induced Acute Dystonia (G24.02)
items: Abnormal prolonged muscle contractions or increased muscle tone (DSM p.812)
Onset within hours to days of starting/increasing D2 blocker or reducing anticholinergic (DSM p.812)
Not better explained by catatonia, primary neurological condition, or tardive dystonia (DSM p.812)

clusters.name: Medication-Induced Acute Akathisia (G25.71)
items: Subjective restlessness and compulsion to move legs (DSM p.813)
At least one observed movement: leg fidgeting/swinging, pacing, rocking from foot to foot (DSM p.813)
Onset within 4 weeks of starting/increasing drug or reducing anticholinergic (DSM p.813)

clusters.name: Medication-Induced Parkinsonism (G21.11 / G21.19)
items: Presence of resting tremor, rigidity, or bradykinesia (DSM p.807-808)
Onset within weeks to months (typically 2-4 weeks to 3 months) of D2 blocker treatment (DSM p.808)
Not better explained by Parkinson's disease, depression, or catatonia (DSM p.808)

criteria.thresholds: Dystonia: hours to 5 days (DSM p.812); Akathisia: within 4 weeks (DSM p.813); Parkinsonism: 2-4 weeks up to 3 months (DSM p.808)

items: Tardive Dystonia (G24.09): Onset after >=3 months exposure; anticholinergics ineffective or worsen condition (DSM p.816)
Psychomotor Agitation: Psychiatric origin, not localized to legs, worsens if antipsychotic discontinued (DSM p.814)
Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS): Onset in evening/at rest, relieved by movement, paresthesias present (DSM p.814, Dulcan p.485)
Idiopathic Parkinson's Disease: Unilateral/asymmetric onset, hyposmia, REM sleep behavior disorder present (DSM p.808)
Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (G21.0): Hyperthermia (>38.0°C), lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, CPK >=4x ULN (DSM p.810)
key_numbers: 3 months minimum drug exposure for Tardive Dyskinesia/Dystonia (1 month if age >=60) (DSM p.815)
3-6 Hz resting tremor frequency in parkinsonism (DSM p.808)
8-12 Hz postural tremor frequency in drug-induced postural tremor (DSM p.817)
>38.0°C (100.4°F) hyperthermia threshold for NMS on at least 2 occasions (DSM p.810)
>=4x upper limit of normal CPK elevation in NMS (DSM p.810)

items: Acute Dystonia / Laryngeal Crisis: Benztropine 1-2mg IM/IV or Diphenhydramine 25-50mg IM/IV (StahlKids p.39, DSM p.812)
Akathisia Management: Reduce D2 blocker dose, Propranolol 30-90mg/day (0.5-1mg/kg/day in kids), Lorazepam, Mirtazapine 15mg (Dulcan p.833, StahlKids p.39)
Parkinsonism Management: Reduce dose, switch to SGA (Quetiapine/Clozapine), Oral Benztropine 1-2mg BID, or Amantadine 100mg BID (StahlNeuro p.166, Dulcan p.833)
NMS Emergency Protocol: Immediately discontinue D2 blocker, ICU supportive care, IV hydration, Dantrolene 1-2.5mg/kg IV q6h, Bromocriptine (DSM p.811, StahlNeuro p.169, Syllabus p.35)
key_numbers: 1-2 mg Benztropine IM/IV dose for acute dystonia (StahlKids p.39)
10-20 minutes typical response time for IM/IV anticholinergic in acute dystonia (StahlNeuro p.169)
30-90 mg/day Propranolol dose for akathisia (Dulcan p.833)
15 mg/day low-dose Mirtazapine for refractory akathisia (Dulcan p.833)
1-2.5 mg/kg IV Dantrolene q6h for NMS (StahlNeuro p.169)

high_yield: D2 occupancy >80% in dorsal striatum triggers EPS, whereas 60%-65% provides antipsychotic efficacy (StahlNeuro p.165)
Acute dystonia peak incidence is 24-48 hours; 90% occur within 5 days of starting or increasing D2 blockers (DSM p.812)
Acute laryngeal dystonia is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate IV Benztropine and airway security (DSM p.812)
Akathisia causes severe subjective distress and dysphoria, leading to a marked increase in suicide risk and aggression (DSM p.814)
Misinterpreting akathisia as psychotic agitation and raising antipsychotic dose causes catastrophic worsening (DSM p.814, Dulcan p.439)
Drug-induced parkinsonism presents with bilateral symmetric signs, unlike idiopathic Parkinson's disease (DSM p.808)
Anticholinergic medications relieve parkinsonism but exacerbate Tardive Dyskinesia (DSM p.816, StahlNeuro p.169)
Propranolol (30-90mg/day) is first-line pharmacotherapy for akathisia; classic anticholinergics are ineffective (Dulcan p.833, StahlKids p.39)
NMS requires immediate cessation of D2 blockers, aggressive cooling, IV hydration, and Dantrolene/Bromocriptine (DSM p.811, Syllabus p.35)
Diphenhydramine in pediatric or neurodevelopmental patients may induce paradoxical agitation (Dulcan p.611-612)
